question: Why does a street sound so strangely hushed right after a fresh, fluffy snowfall?
alternative_answers: Air pockets in snow absorb sound
source_excerpt: Snow is going to be porous, and typically porous materials such as fibers and foams, and things of that sort, absorb sound pretty well.

extra.why_interesting: Nearly everyone has noticed the eerie hush after a snowfall, but most people assume it's just because fewer cars and people are out. The real reason is physical: fluffy snow behaves like acoustic foam in a recording studio.
extra.verification_notes: Fresh snow is porous and absorbs sound, which is the standard explanation for post-snowfall quiet (https://accuweather.com/en/weather-news/why-does-it-become-so-quiet-after-a-fresh-snowfall/352439).

explanation: Fresh snow is mostly air trapped between ice crystals, so it soaks up sound like the foam on a recording studio wall. Once it melts and refreezes into a hard crust, it reflects sound and the hush is gone.

question: From the ground a rainbow always looks like an arch, but pilots flying above the rain sometimes see it as what shape?
source_excerpt: From above the Earth such as in an aeroplane, it is sometimes possible to see a rainbow as a full circle.

extra.why_interesting: Everyone 'knows' a rainbow is an arch with two ends, and folklore even puts gold at the end. The player can reason toward the answer by picturing what changes when you're high above the ground, and the reveal that rainbows never really have ends is a delightful 'huh, really?'.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia's Rainbow article confirms that from an aeroplane a rainbow can sometimes be seen as a full circle (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rainbow).

explanation: A rainbow is really a ring of light centred on the spot directly opposite the sun, and on the ground the earth simply blocks the bottom half. So there is no end of the rainbow, and no pot of gold either.
